tools.name: get_agent_code
tools.description: Returns the full source of one agent from the registry, by its name (e.g. @bill/neuron_agent), so it can be read or adapted.

tools.name: use_agent_here

Returns a short Python runner so you can run the agent in this chat with your own Python tool on the user's own data (pasted text, an uploaded spreadsheet, a list). Nothing to install. tools.name: how_to_run_agent
tools.description: Optional, for later: how to keep an agent running on the user's own computer with the free Brainstem. Only offer this after the user has used the agent in the chat and wants to keep it.

tools.name: request_service
tools.description: Use when the person wants something none of these tools can do and says yes to passing the request on. Records only the request text they agree to send (no name or contact). Ask before calling it.

findings.title: Description issues instructions to the model
findings.detail: Description of "request_service" contains imperative instructions directed at the AI assistant rather than describing the tool. This is the core tool-poisoning technique.

findings.remediation: Treat the server as untrusted; the model may obey embedded instructions.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta: untrusted input + private data + external sink
findings.detail: Server "mcp" exposes tools that together enable an exfiltration flow. Untrusted content: use_agent_here · Private data: find_agents, request_service · Public sink: request_service · Destructive: use_agent_here, how_to_run_agent.

evidence.snippet: Untrusted content: use_agent_here · Private data: find_agents, request_service · Public sink: request_service · Destructive: use_agent_here, how_to_run_agent

findings.remediation: Do not co-install these capabilities under one trust boundary; an injected comment/email can steer the model to exfiltrate via the sink tool.
